text: As the years slipped away and both of them grew older, May began to suffer from a mysterious illness, and Marcher, with a sharp chill of fear, realized that she might die before the Beast appeared. <break time="0.8s" /> What troubled him most was not the thought of losing her but the fear that she would miss the end of their long watch, as if a spectator should leave just before the curtain fell. <break time="0.8s" /> Watching her closely, he came to suspect that she had already guessed the nature of his fate, and one evening he begged her to tell him whether she knew something that he did not. <break time="0.8s" /> Her answer, gentle but firm, was that she would never tell him, and her eyes, resting on him with infinite patience, seemed to hold a knowledge that was almost too painful to bear. <break time="0.8s" /> For the first time, Marcher was haunted by a new and sharper dread, namely that the great event might never come at all, and that his long watch might end in nothing. <break time="0.8s" /> One April evening he came to her house and found her sitting very still, dressed with unusual care, so pale and composed that she seemed less a sick woman than a serene and impenetrable sphinx. <break time="0.8s" /> As they talked once more of the thing that was to come, she said to him softly, with a strange brightness in her face, It is never too late.
